title: Bread and Butter Pudding
subtitle: Buttered bread soaked in vanilla custard and baked until golden
excerpt: Sliced white bread buttered generously, layered in a dish with sultanas, then soaked in a vanilla egg custard and baked until set, golden, and just catching at the edges. The essential British nursery pudding.
sourceNotes: Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845), bread and butter pudding as a classic British nursery dish. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. The dish has been made in British kitchens since at least the seventeenth century as a way of using stale bread.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble the pudding up to 4 hours ahead and leave it to soak in the fridge. Bake from cold, adding 5 minutes to the cooking time.

glossaryTerms.definition: A roasting tin filled with hot water in which a baking dish is set. The water bath moderates the oven heat so the custard sets slowly and evenly without curdling or becoming rubbery.

content.text: Bread and butter pudding is buttered bread baked in a vanilla egg custard until golden on top and just set in the middle. It should tremble slightly when you take it out of the oven. The centre finishes setting as it rests. This dish uses a
to keep the custard soft and creamy rather than rubbery.

items.prepNote: slices, about 400 g, slightly stale is fine

content.text: Butter each slice of {{bread-white}} bread with {{unsalted-butter}} of softened butter. Cut each slice in half diagonally.
Arrange the triangles in a buttered baking dish in overlapping rows, buttered-side up. Scatter {{sultanas}} of sultanas between the layers if using.

Whisk together {{eggs}} eggs, {{caster-sugar}} of caster sugar, and {{vanilla-extract}} of vanilla extract. Warm {{whole-milk}} of milk and {{double-cream}} of double cream in a saucepan until steaming but not boiling. Pour the hot liquid slowly onto the egg mixture, whisking as you go.
Pour the custard over the bread. Press the bread down gently so it absorbs the liquid. Leave to soak for at least 30 minutes. Sprinkle {{demerara-sugar}} of demerara sugar over the top if using.

Heat the oven to 170 degrees C. Place the baking dish inside a roasting tin. Pour boiling water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the sides of the baking dish. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the top is golden and just set with a slight tremor in the centre.
Remove the baking dish from the water bath and rest for 10 minutes before serving. Serve warm.

rows.symptom: Custard is rubbery and set hard
rows.cause: Baked at too high a temperature or without a water bath
rows.fix: The bain-marie is essential. Without it the edges overcook before the centre sets. Keep the oven at 170 degrees C.

rows.symptom: Custard is still completely liquid after 35 minutes
rows.cause: Oven temperature too low, or not enough soaking time before baking
rows.fix: Check the oven temperature. The pudding is done when the top is golden and the custard just holds its shape when pressed gently in the centre.

rows.symptom: Top is soggy rather than golden
rows.cause: Bread too fresh or over-soaked, oven temperature too low
rows.fix: Make sure the protruding bread tips are brushed with a little extra butter. Switch to grill for the last 3 minutes to crisp the top.

rows.cause: Ratio of eggs to cream is off, or vanilla not added
rows.fix: Use the recipe ratio. Make sure the vanilla extract is included: it covers the egg smell.

content.text: Bread and butter pudding appears in British cookery books since the seventeenth century. It was a way to use stale bread. Victorian cookery writer Mrs Beeton included it in her 1861 cookbook under nursery puddings. By the twentieth century it was linked to British school dinners. High-end restaurants revived it in the 1990s. It is now a classic British comfort dessert.
